column16: Black Horse (now called Cappall Dubh) is a pub in Aldgate, London, open every day from 11am to 1am. The page highlights its fresh energy at the same location and points visitors to an Events page for a full lineup. It also mentions functions and parties, with space for birthdays, work dos and other gatherings. The venue is described as having sports on TV, a dartboard, and great music, with examples of ticketed events listed in the “Upcoming Events” section.

Commercial Tavern is a Victorian corner pub in Spitalfields (142–144 Commercial Street, London E1 6NU) with large windows and eccentric decoration. It features an upstairs cocktail bar with velvet booths and curated playlists. The venue focuses on rotating craft beers, expertly mixed cocktails, and a burger offering from Meat Stop, described as dry-aged British beef with house-made sauces. The page also highlights “Games” and a “hidden Fitzrovia favourite” vibe for the cocktail bar, making it suitable for dates and discreet meetups.

Set on Back Church Lane in East London, this long-running boozer is known for a strong line-up of local beers and proper pub food—especially Pie Minister pies. Expect a friendly, no-fuss atmosphere with space for meetings or celebrations, plus a quiz night for regular fun. There are two beer gardens for warmer days, and you can settle in with board games as well as a welcoming crowd. A classic local spot with a bit of character and plenty to keep you there after the first pint.

column16: Duke Of Somerset London is a city pub with decadent decor and a large external beer garden. It offers a great range of craft beers and premium spirits, including an extensive gin range, plus a cocktail menu. The venue is well set up for sport viewing, with 14 internal TVs and external viewing, and it lists Sky Sports and TNT Sports with HD screens. Facilities include Wi‑Fi and accessible toilets, and there’s a dartboard. Live music is listed, and children are welcome with a family policy of no children after 7pm on Thursday and Friday nights.

The Duke of Wellington at 12 Toynbee Street (E17NE) is promoting “game nights” and big-screen football viewing. The page highlights FIFA World Cup fixtures and encourages visitors to come with a pint for non-stop football action. There’s also a booking contact email shown for booking inquiries.

The Goodman’s Field is a Wetherspoon pub in 87–91 Mansell Street, Tower Hamlets, London. It’s open daily from 8:00am until 11:00pm, with children under 18 only allowed on the premises between 8:00am and 10:00pm. Facilities include Wi‑Fi, TV screens and a licensed outside deck area, plus step-free access. The pub offers children’s meals (including pizzas) for £4.99 and £5.75, served with a drink and fruit. The page also includes a detailed local history of the surrounding land and mentions guest ale and craft tasting notes, along with a range of spritz cocktails.

Grapeshots is a popular local wine bar tucked away down a narrow Victorian passage near Liverpool Street. It has a warm, cosy atmosphere with wood panelling and candlelit tables, plus antique curiosities and historic wine artefacts collected over decades. Guests can enjoy a diverse wine list and an interesting selection of craft beers, alongside modern British cooking on the food menu using seasonal ingredients that are UK and, where possible, locally sourced. The downstairs dining area suits group dining and drinks parties, and the venue can be hired for private events. It also hosts wine tastings and live music as part of its upcoming events.

column16: The Kings Stores is a vibrant, “hidden gem” pub in Whitechapel, nestled between the City and Spitalfields market. It has a diverse crowd and offers a lively World Cup atmosphere, with Sky Sports and TNT Sports. The venue serves a la carte dining and pub classics such as fish and chips, plus small plates and sharing dishes. There are private rooms for parties, meetings and get-togethers, each with its own private bar. Facilities include disabled access, family friendly features, WiFi, and functions. The page also promotes a Spring–Summer menu and Friday Prosecco offers.

The Knave of Clubs is a historic East End pub on the corner of Bethnal Green Road and Club Row, brought back to life after being closed for 30 years. It’s open daily and serves Guinness alongside oysters and rotisserie chicken, with food available all day. The pub offers beers, wine and cocktails, and reservations are available online with walk-ins welcome. The venue also features One Club Row above the pub, inspired by New York taverns and Paris bistros, with long lunches, late dinners, dining at the bar, people watching, and two private dining rooms for parties.

Leman Street Tavern is a pub in Aldgate, described as “Aldgate’s shining gem” where the City of London meets the East End. It offers a heated, covered beer garden and a range of spaces for dining, drinks, and celebrations, including a fully private room called “The Chambers” and an outdoor terrace. Food is a key focus, with “Best of British Classics,” seasonal menus, and “Legendary Sundays” featuring Sunday roasts and double-egg Yorkshire puddings. The venue also promotes World Cup 2026 viewing “across our screens,” with big-match atmosphere. Food is served from 12:00–21:00 on Sundays, and the pub is open Sunday 12:00–22:00.

The London Hospital Tavern (LHT) was built for the builders of the hospital that shares its name, over 150 years ago, as a place to enjoy a pint after work. Today it continues that tradition for NHS staff and the local community. The pub offers food via a menu you can check before you arrive, alongside a wide selection of beer, wines and spirits, including a cocktail of the month and constantly rotating ales. There’s also a house bottled beer with 10p from every bottle sold going to the Air Ambulance Charity. Upstairs, the Mosaic bar hosts midweek live entertainment such as comedy, storytelling, improv and jazz, with more event nights at weekends.

Ninety One is a modern pub on Brick Lane, set within the Old Brewmaster's House of the Truman Brewery. It’s described as a cosy neighbourhood hangout with a warm, laid-back atmosphere. The venue is set up for dining alongside quality live music, which then flows into signature DJ nights that run late, with the dance floor coming alive on weekends. Food is available via a dedicated Food Menu and a Sunday roast menu. Opening times are listed for Wednesday through Sunday.

The Pride of Spitalfields London is an authentic East End pub just off Brick Lane, offering traditional vibes and a warm, inviting atmosphere. The page highlights an exceptional beer selection with cask ales and well-kept pints, including a cracking Guinness at notably reasonable prices. Inside, it’s described as cozy and unpretentious, with worn carpets, comfy seats, and a roaring fire, creating a classic “public house” feel. There’s also mention of a lively standing crowd and an outside patio/street area that can be packed on sunny days. The venue is presented as a community hub with piano nights mentioned as a regular feature.

The Princess of Prussia is a traditional, historic pub in Whitechapel, close to Tower Bridge and the Tower of London. Inside, it features original ornate ceramic mouldings, cornices and fascia tiles, with a cosy traditional bar serving real ales from Shepherd Neame. It offers lunchtime food with a Thai twist (including Jungle Curry and Drunken Noodles) plus fish and chips, available 12–3pm daily. There’s also an alfresco experience in a secret, covered and heated beer garden, where food and drink are served up to 10pm.

Step into a classic London boozer near Tower Hill, with a warm, welcoming feel and plenty of local character. Expect a lively hangout built around pub games—pool table, dart boards—and an eclectic jukebox for background music. There’s also a spacious beer garden for unwinding with a pint. The menu is described as classic pub fare, ideal for a relaxed dine-in while you play. Drinks include well-known lagers and regular ales, with occasional special releases, and the bar team is noted for friendly service.

column16: The Astronomer is a pub in one of London’s most vibrant areas, drawing style inspiration from the night sky and offering a lively atmosphere. It serves fresh, well-kept cask ales, craft beers and cocktails, alongside a dining menu of refined pub classics made with fresh, seasonal ingredients. The Rocket Room downstairs can cater for private events including business meetings, weddings and birthdays. The venue also highlights board games, free WiFi and accessibility features, and it welcomes families and assistance dogs. Food is served daily with set food serving times.

column16: The Bell is an independently owned Victorian pub on the fringes of the City on Middlesex Street, near Petticoat Lane Market and Jack the Ripper territory. It’s easy to reach from Liverpool Street and Aldgate underground stations, and is known for a mixed crowd of local residents and office workers. The pub is eclectically decorated and features two function rooms, including a games room with a pool table, darts and table football, plus an upstairs function room for rehearsals, meetings, performances and screenings. There’s also street art updates. Food is available via Detroit Pizza delivery or by bringing food from the local market, alongside craft beer on tap and in fridges.

The Blind Beggar is a “wet-led” pub in Whitechapel, London, known for its regularly updated beer lineup and wide range of beer styles, from lagers to craft ales. The pub has a long history, including being the former brewery tap of the Manns Albion brewery and being built in 1894 on an earlier inn site. It’s also noted for its famous cultural connections, and hosts events such as “The Krays: Ronnie, Reggie and Me” with Fred Dinenage. The venue features an award-winning beer garden with a decked pergola, heated outside bar, and comfortable seating.

Nestled at 139 Leman Street in the vibrant Whitechapel district of London, the Brown Bear stands as one of the East End's most storied public houses. This Grade II listed Victorian gem, with its striking blue facade and bear motifs, has served as a social anchor for over two centuries. Its history mirrors the area's transformation—from 18th-century industrial bustle to the gritty underbelly of Victorian London, through wartime resilience and into the multicultural hub it is today.

column16: The Buxton is described as a small wine bar and hotel with big character at the foot of Brick Lane in London. The site highlights an “Eat & Drink” offering with a bar menu curated with working relationships with brewers and winemakers. It also offers accommodation: 15 simple, paired-back bedrooms for the modern traveller, with room booking and an email contact for queries. The page notes the venue is open now and provides opening hours (7AM to 11PM).

The Crown and Shuttle is an old-school East-End boozer on Shoreditch High Street in East London. The venue offers food via a “Daily Menu” and has drink menus, with opening hours that vary by day and can change for events and sports matches. It’s set up for groups, with table areas for drinks and private spaces for parties. The pub also hosts entertainment upstairs at Filthy Fanny’s, including weekly life drawing classes, life music, comedians, and other “louche entertainment”. There are references to a beer garden, and the site highlights seasonal events and match-related viewing.

The George Tavern is a legendary public house in London’s east end, known for its thriving artistic community. Owner Pauline Forster has spent the last decade turning The George into an arts, music and performance venue with an international reputation. The pub offers live music from a range of artists, alongside the comfort of a classic East-End boozer. It also serves fresh hand-stretched pizza in the garden, with the kitchen open Wednesday to Sunday from 6pm til late. The venue includes a cosy dining area at the back of a patio and has a distinctive “Save The George” design associated with London’s indie-music scene.

Set on a prominent corner in Spitalfields, this Grade II listed pub is a rare inter-war “improved” design with a largely intact interior. Expect a warm, historic feel with separate bar spaces including a Saloon Bar entrance on Hanbury Street, plus original features like fielded panelling, stained glass and fixed bench seating. The venue is closely tied to Truman’s Brewery and its 1930s style, with neo-Georgian frontage and original neon signage. A great choice for a relaxed drink in a building with real architectural and local-art history behind it.

column16: Set inside Spitalfields Market, this Young’s gastropub brings industrial East London energy with a rustic wooden bar and a large covered terrace for drinks overlooking the bustle. Expect freshly poured pints alongside ales, fine wines and premium spirits, plus hearty British pub grub—think grilled steaks, burgers and Sunday roasts. A great stop for after-work crowds near Liverpool Street, with a beer-garden style terrace designed for lingering.

column16: The Gun in Spitalfields is an East London community hub by Spitalfields Market, described as an “East London favourite since the 17th Century”. It offers a craft drinks selection alongside seasonally rotating menus inspired by British produce, including sharing plates and a noted Sunday roast. The venue also runs events such as Sunday roasts, cocktail masterclasses, and DJ nights (Thursday to Saturday). It has kitchen times listed and serves food daily with Sunday kitchen hours ending earlier. For sports fans, it mentions “big screens” and “every kick live” for World Cup match nights.

The Half Moon is a pub at 213–223 Mile End Road, Mile End (Tower Hamlets). The building began as a former Methodist chapel built in 1900, later taken over by the Half Moon Theatre Company in 1977, and eventually converted into The Half Moon several years after the theatre closed in 1990. The venue offers Wi‑Fi, TV screens, and a licensed outside deck, with step-free access and baby changing facilities. Opening times run from 8:00am to late most days, with children under 18 only allowed on the premises between 8:00am and 9:00pm. Food and drinks can be ordered via the Wetherspoon app.

The Horn of Plenty is a small neighbourhood pub in the heart of Stepney Green, about 100 yards from the station. It’s described as intimate and cosy, with a huge selection of East End produce and local breweries, wines and spirits. The pub has 2 big screens/projectors showing football, rugby and other sporting events, plus a weekly quiz (Tuesdays) and themed quiz nights monthly. There are also NHS & student discounts on Wednesdays, a few boardgames, and a “cracking playlist”. Opening hours are listed for each day, and reservations are mentioned.

The Light Bar is an independent bar and dining venue set in an old Victorian power station built in 1893, in Shoreditch, London. It spans three floors and is described as a modern bar and restaurant with “good times.” The page highlights new menus, later hours, and offers events such as bottomless brunch with world-class DJs, a Friday happy hour (2-4-1 cocktails between 4pm–8pm), and DJ nights every Friday and Saturday.

The Oliver Conquest dates from the mid 19th century and was originally called The Garrick, attached to the first Garrick Theatre behind the pub. The venue highlights a strong gin focus, with a current range of over 120 different bottles and new varieties added daily. There are featured gin and spirit selections including Japanese Gin with botanicals such as yuzu and juniper, spiced rum from the Sairen range, and a Black & Gold 11yo bourbon. The page also promotes booking a table and ordering via the site locator.

The Owl & the Pussycat is a popular Shoreditch pub on Redchurch Street, described as the “soul of Shoreditch” with an old-skool heart. It offers a food menu of hearty pub favourites, sharing boards and nibbly bits, plus beers on draft and seasonal cocktails. Sundays are a highlight, with epic Sunday roasts, bottomless Yorkies and unlimited gravy, plus a “Crumble Guy” mention. There’s an all-season, heated and covered beer garden at the rear, and the first-floor “Jago” space for food, drinks and cocktails. The pub also shows World Cup 2026 games live on big screens in proper pub style.

The Peacock is a traditional Irish pub in the back streets of East London, described as one of the last remaining original east end boozers in Stepney. Built in 1881, it survived WWII and was nicknamed “The Copper’s Pub” due to its location opposite the Thames Magistrate Court and Police Station. After redevelopment and refurbishment, it reopened in 2023 while keeping original features and character. The pub offers a menu of traditional Irish food (including stews and fish and chips mentioned) alongside a wide selection of drinks such as cask ales, craft beers, and over 20 Irish whiskeys. Live Irish music runs regularly, with live music every Friday and quiz night every Saturday.

The Running Horse Aldgate is a bar in Aldgate, close to Aldgate East station, offering after-work pints, cocktails, and a food menu built around rotisserie cooking. Guests can enjoy craft beer from rotating taps and options like rotisserie chicken, smash burgers, and Sunday roasts (dry-aged beef rib, Cotswold white chicken, or Old Spot pork belly). The kitchen focuses on fire and flavour, including a 12-hour brine for free-range chicken. Sundays run 12pm–4pm, with a “Bottomless Roasts” offer including unlimited Prosecco and Bellinis for 90 minutes. The venue also supports group bookings with semi-private spaces and full venue hire, plus match-day viewing for major tournaments.

The Shoreditch Arms is a lively pub in the heart of Shoreditch, serving food alongside craft beers, wines and spirits. During the week it offers lunch options and small plates, with a menu that includes classic pub food and cocktails. The venue also promotes “Bar Kick” in the basement as a gameday experience for live sport and sporting-and-gaming good times. There’s a hidden secret cocktail bar upstairs with velvet booths and curated playlists, described as a plush, low-lit escape. The page also highlights games and a private hire setup with an outdoor area and screens.

The Star by Liverpool Street is a karaoke-focused venue near Liverpool Street Station, with five private karaoke booths/rooms and themed spaces designed for singing into the early hours. It also offers two function rooms and a karaoke bar, plus regular karaoke nights, open karaoke, and events like Pub Quiz and 80s Musical Bingo Bottomless Brunch. Food is available via the dedicated Firestarter restaurant, with bar food including speciality burgers and sliders, sides and small plates using smoky, coal-roasted cooking techniques. The venue also highlights “two floors of the best live sports action”.

The Ten Bells is a historic East End London beer-factory pub in Spitalfields, described as a bustling, candle-lit social hub with a rock ’n’ roll twist. It serves an eclectic range of quality beers and an extensive cocktail menu, with a cocktail bar upstairs offering a curated selection of classics and Ten Bells signature cocktails. The venue is spread across three floors and is positioned as a great place to host events, just five minutes from Liverpool Street Station.

The White Hart, Whitechapel is a historic pub standing since 1750 and rebuilt around 1900, with a “second life” brought into the 21st century. It offers a relaxed, characterful atmosphere with craft beers (Hertfordshire brewed cask and keg), cocktails, popular wines and traditional British fayre, including a Sunday roast. Food is served alongside a range of menus (main, Sunday, kids, buffet) and allergen information. There’s an upstairs area used for a weekly quiz and private hire, plus outside tables for enjoying a pint while watching the world go by near Whitechapel station. The venue also runs events such as open mic night and quiz nights.

column16: The White Swan is a traditional pub in the heart of the City, described as a “hidden gem” in Aldgate East on the historic grounds of the old Half Moon Theatre. It serves a selection of Shepherd Neame beers, including rich seasonal ales, alongside an enviable wine list and an impressive spirits collection. The pub offers a welcoming atmosphere for relaxed evenings with friends or memorable meet-ups with colleagues. It also provides events and private hire, including a cosy function room for up to 25 guests and the option to hire the entire venue exclusively, with support for audio-visual equipment and whiteboards.

Williams Ale & Cider House is an East London pub in Whitechapel, tucked between the City and Spitalfields. It’s known for an extensive ale and cider collection, plus a delicious seasonal menu. The pub promotes a lively World Cup atmosphere and offers cask beer, including a guaranteed IPA and house bitter from national and local brewers. Food options range from bar snacks to burgers, and there are facilities including WiFi and a dog-friendly welcome. The venue also has darts, and it offers table booking and menu viewing online.

Tucked inside Wilton’s Music Hall, this intimate Mahogany Bar feels deeply East End—decor that looks wonderfully worn-in, plus a side room with a small exhibition on the building’s history. After a wider complex refurb, there’s more space to settle in while keeping the atmosphere. Expect a well-stocked bar with a solid selection of wine and ales, and an upstairs cocktail bar if the main area gets busy. A great pick for a characterful drink before or around events at this historic music hall setting.

column16: The Coach and Horses is an independent East London pub with roots since 1863 (and the current venue since 2018). It serves locally brewed beers, real ales, cocktails, Nepalese street food and Sunday roasts. The pub is family and dog-friendly, with a partially covered beer garden. There’s live music on Friday nights from 8pm, quiz nights, and live sport shown on six big screens indoors and outdoors—covering major football and rugby tournaments. It’s also a good spot for parties and whole-pub hire, with table bookings available.

Set back from Lea Bridge Road in East London, this characterful pub in Leyton mixes a homely local feel with event-ready spaces. Expect a colourful bar with craft beers, real ales and a strong wine selection, plus proper pub food—burgers, chicken wings, salads and a traditional Sunday roast. There’s also a garden area with covered seating, ideal for catching the sun. For bigger occasions, the whole venue can be hired, including a pool room that opens onto the gardens, making it a flexible spot for celebrations.

column16: King William IV is an “East End original” pub, beautifully reborn under the stewardship of Walthamstow’s Exale Brewing. It pours 14 lines of tank-fresh beer and cask ale, plus cocktails and a curated wine list, in a laid-back, old-school setting. There’s a private events room and a beer garden, and the pub shows live sports for football, rugby and boxing nights. Food is available via Short Road Pizza, serving award-winning pizzas and Italian small plates. The venue also runs weekly deals and hosts events such as DJ nights, quiz nights, comedy and pottery classes. Kitchen hours are listed and children are welcome until 7pm.

A football supporters’ club bar in Leyton, set in the redeveloped stand by Oliver Road. It’s a real-ale specialist with a rotating line-up of micros, multiple handpumps and regular beer festivals. Expect a friendly, community feel on matchdays, with home and away fans mixing, plus TV screens showing early Premier League kick-offs and Sky Sports results. There’s also outdoor overspill seating on a raised area when the weather’s good, and guests can be signed in (CAMRA members admitted). Food is mentioned only as a “filled roll” in one review, so it’s best thought of as a beer-first venue.

column16: Queer Brewing Project’s taproom in Leyton, East London, is on a peaceful industrial estate near Lea Bridge Station. It serves beer fresh from the brewery on 8 dedicated lines, alongside cans, cider, natural wine and snacks, with alcohol-free and gluten-free options available. The taproom welcomes dogs and children, is wheelchair accessible and step-free, and offers the option to order pizza to your table via local pizzeria Proud Mary. There are regular offers such as £5 pints from 4–6pm every Friday, plus events including a women’s Six Nations screening.

column16: At the top of Leyton’s High Road, this imposing pub keeps a classic feel while making room for a working brewery at the back. Expect a big focus on beer: a rotating lineup with experimental brews, plus traditional cider and perry. The space is now largely one main drinking area, with original fittings and standout wall mirrors in the bar. It’s a lively stop for anyone who likes trying different pours, from core favourites to specials, alongside regular nights of music, comedy and interactive games.

column16: Heathcote & Star is a lovingly restored pub in Leytonstone, described as having the biggest beer garden in the area. It offers an impressive drinks menu and food from The Dragon Flame, including BBQ dishes and Sunday roasts. The pub is positioned as a community spot for after-work drinks, with a games room and screens for live sport. It also hosts regular events such as pub quizzes, cocktail offers, and family film Fridays, alongside drink tastings, food nights, and beer pong tournaments. The venue offers private hire, including function rooms and booths, with options for conferencing and club nights.

column16: Leytonstone Tavern is an independent, community-focused neighbourhood pub and dining room in Leytonstone. It offers sustainably sourced, ethically reared produce alongside hand-picked craft beers and ciders. The venue is known for award-winning burgers, tacos and other street-food style dishes, with sample menus and regularly updated dishes. Kitchen hours run through the week with extended evening service. The pub also hosts events such as weddings, wakes, birthdays and BBQs, with an events team that creates bespoke experiences. There are also regular weekday offers like local pints, taco Tuesdays, wing Wednesdays and burger deals, plus takeaway beers.

column16: The Sir Alfred Hitchcock Hotel in Leytonstone E11 offers a bar, restaurant and hotel, plus a venue for events. The “What’s On” section highlights regular food offerings such as Sunday Roast every Sunday (12:00 to 17:00), Thursday Steak Nights in the evening, and seasonal menus including a new menu from 17th January, a set Christmas menu from 20th November, kids menu, and a Christmas Day menu (25/12/25). Reservations can be made by calling 0208 530 3724, booking a room, or booking a table by email.

Bell Leytonstone is a pub on 468 High Road, Leytonstone (London E11 3HN) with long opening hours. It’s positioned as a sports-focused venue, promising to show every match live and highlighting live tournament viewing such as World Cup 2026. The site also promotes “unbeatable drink offers” and mentions facilities including Wi‑Fi, HD screens, TNT Sports and Sky Sports. Live entertainment is also listed, alongside a newsletter sign-up for community news and updates.

The Birkbeck Tavern is a sports-focused pub with Sky Sports, BT Sport, Racing UK and At the Races, showing premiership and international football, rugby, cricket and golf. It also offers pool and darts, with free pool on Monday and Thursday. There’s a function room for birthdays, weddings, anniversaries and wakes, with a private bar and a separate garden area. The pub serves beer, wines and spirits, including a wide range of real ales and cocktails, plus wines and premium spirits. A hidden outdoor beer garden with seating is available all year, and BBQs are mentioned at weekends.

The Bull is a friendly local pub in Wanstead (E11), just 100 yards from Wanstead Tube Station. It has a sunny beer garden “suntrap” with parasols, open every day until 11pm. The pub serves fresh, delicious food five days a week using locally sourced, sustainable ingredients, and it also offers a kids’ menu every day. Families are welcome, with “Little Bulls” welcome when accompanied by adults. Dogs are included too, with dog beds and bowls, dog snacks at the bar, and doggy roasts on Sundays (dogs kept on a lead).

The Cuckfield is an iconic London pub on Wanstead High Street, offering a memorable drinking and dining experience. It serves fresh, flavoursome home-cooked food alongside a diverse drinks menu. The page also highlights options such as a relaxed lunch, Sunday roast, family dinner and brunch, and provides online table booking and gift cards. Opening hours are listed for each day, and the address is 31 High Street, Wanstead (E11 2AA).

The Duke is a Wanstead neighbourhood pub and dining room offering lunch and dinner, plus Sunday roasts and a rotating set of specials such as a Wednesday homemade pie and Thursday steak night. The site also highlights coffee from Perky Blenders and regular drink offers including a Monday club and a Mon/Tues burger deal. Entertainment features include DJ nights on Fridays and live music on the 1st Sunday of every month (DukeBox Sundays). The page also promotes events like neighbourhood social nights, happy hour, and themed occasions such as World Cup viewing and quizzes.

The George and Dragon in Wanstead offers a refined pub experience with expertly crafted British dishes, real ales, excellent wines and exciting cocktails. There are spaces to party including a Ballroom and Cocktail Bar, plus an iconic stage in the Club Room that has hosted artists such as Ed Sheeran and Sam Smith. The Cyclist is a modern British pub in Balham, just across the road from Balham Station. It offers an all-day food offering during the week, plus Saturday brunch and Sunday lunch at weekends. Food includes a Burger Shack, pub classics and seasonal menus, with Sunday roast dinners served by Head Chef Raff. The venue is also described as a rugby HQ and sports spot for major tournaments, with big screens and match-day atmosphere. Events listed include weekly quiz nights and Women’s Six Nations fixtures.

The Grove is a pub in Balham, tucked just off Balham High Street, established in 1870. It offers “Food & Drink” with classic British pub menus that change with the seasons, including vegan and allergen-friendly options, plus lighter bites, coffee and pastries. It’s a popular spot for big-match rugby screenings and Sunday roasts, and there’s a sun-soaked beer garden and light, airy indoor spaces. The venue also hosts parties and events, with flexible indoor spaces and seasonal sharing boards and summer plates.

We’re a proper community pub, proudly serving Balham locals and anyone who fancies a great pint just a short stroll from Clapham South and Wandsworth Common. There are also sections for a drinks menu and events/functions, and it offers a “Friends of The Crossing” deal of 15% off your food bill Monday to Thursday. The pub offers a “delicious menu” with classics and seasonal specials, including British comfort food such as pies, Sunday roasts, sharing platters, and options including vegan, vegetarian and non-gluten dishes. It also has a beer garden (weather permitting) and is dog- and family-friendly. Sports fans can watch live Sky and TNT Sports, with big-screen match viewing and fixtures listed.

column16: The Warwick Arms in Kensington is a traditional-style pub tucked between Olympia and Earl’s Court. It’s known for hearty ales, including fresh cask ales, and friendly, old-fashioned service. At mealtimes it offers home-cooked North Indian cuisine (“Indian Dream”), alongside British pub classics like fish & chips and homemade pies, plus lighter lunch options such as wraps and smaller portions. The pub features include food served, outside seating, a real fire, and paid parking nearby. It also welcomes children aged 8 and over, and provides menu links and food times for dining.

A lively blues bar in the heart of London’s Kingly Street area, built around live performances and a welcoming, music-first atmosphere. Expect comfort-food classics alongside a bar offering, with options for those who prefer non-alcoholic drinks too. It’s a great stop for an evening out where the soundtrack is part of the experience—good tunes paired with hearty bites.

column16: Cahoots Ticket Hall is an all-new 1940s black market pub on Soho’s Kingly Street. It’s open every day from noon until late, with a laid-back, classic 1940s British pub atmosphere. The Scoundrels serve draught beers, pale ales, cocktails, wines and spirits. There’s a spacious outdoor drinking area on Kingly Street (walk-ins only for the outdoor terrace). Lunch is available with a lunchtime menu of classic British pub dishes such as beer-battered cod, bangers & mash and lunchtime sarnies, with bookings 12pm–3.45pm and last orders for lunch at 4.30pm. The venue also offers private party hire with vintage posters, high-level seating and a giant station clock.

The Blue Posts is a historic pub in Soho, described as part of Soho’s fabric since the 1720s. It’s close to Carnaby Street and Regent Street, with a traditional pub feel and a “new look” interior that pays homage to its history. The venue offers a bountiful bar with well-kept cask ales, craft beers, wines, cocktails, and hot drinks. Food is available with a menu covering pub snacks, sharers, starters, sandwiches, mains and puddings, plus lunch options and a Sunday roast theme. Facilities include a beer garden, WiFi, and functions, and the pub is dog friendly.

The Clachan is a historic pub in Soho, described as being in the heart of London on Kingly Street, just off Regent Street. The page highlights a focus on “perfect pints” and “unbeatable pies”, with British pub classic menus and tempting dishes. It also mentions options to book a table, order at the table, and order for collection. The venue is positioned near central London attractions, including Oxford Circus Underground Station (a three-minute walk).

The Glass Blower Piccadilly is a family-friendly, dog-friendly pub in Soho, originally a red brick pub. It’s less than five minutes from Piccadilly Circus tube station and close to shops. The venue offers a menu of pub food including small plates and hearty pub classics, with highlights such as Sunday Roast. There are facilities including WiFi, takeaway, and offers functions. The page also mentions booking tables and functions, plus “big screens at the ready” for major events like the World Cup.

The Leicester Arms Piccadilly is a historic corner pub in Piccadilly, first licensed in 1725. It’s described as a relaxing place to “relax and revive,” with a family-friendly welcome and a dog-friendly policy. Food is a key part of the offer, including a seasonal specials menu, “Delicious Pub Food,” and a Sunday Roast with classic trimmings. The pub is set up for sports fans, with Sky Sports and TNT Sports, and it promotes live football and Six Nations rugby screenings. Facilities mentioned include WiFi, disabled facilities, takeaway, and function rooms for meetings, birthdays and events.

A cosy, oak-panelled Samuel Smith’s pub on busy Kingly Street in Soho, with a working fireplace and a historic feel. It’s laid out across front and back rooms (two floors), giving you both snug corners and a livelier rear space. Expect well-kept beers from Yorkshire breweries and a straightforward pint-and-chat vibe—no music or shouting, just proper pub atmosphere. Outdoor tables are mentioned as popular, making it a good stop after shopping for a relaxed drink and classic pub comfort food like fish and chips.

column16: The Wigmore is a modern British tavern with a luxury twist, set in a former banking hall. Inspired by classic British public houses, it offers a warm, social space for drinking, dining and gathering, with a menu overseen by Michel Roux featuring hearty British dishes reimagined with a refined touch. The venue serves wines on tap, house punches, ‘hoptails’, cask ales and craft beers, plus a signature brew called “Saison”. Located on Regent Street in London’s West End, it’s suitable for everything from lunch to lively evenings. There are also multiple event spaces, including an outdoor terrace (“The Hatch”).

The City of Quebec Marylebone is an Art Deco LGBTQIA+ pub and a long-standing cornerstone of London’s gay community since 1946. It’s known for a vibrant venue with a stage for cabaret and live events, including drag performances. The pub offers food alongside drinks, with menus and dish highlights such as small plates and pizzas. There’s also a beer garden for outdoor drinks (weather permitting). Facilities mentioned include disabled facilities, WiFi, and offers/functions, plus it’s dog friendly.

The Spread Eagle Mayfair is a pub in Mayfair where you can take a moment away from the city. It originally stood on Oxford Street from the 17th century, then was rebuilt set back in 1955. The venue offers space to sit outside and watch the world go by, and it’s known for food at the heart of the experience, including pub classics and a traditional Sunday roast. It also has facilities for functions and is set up for sports viewing, with Sky Sports and TNT Sports, plus live match screenings such as rugby and live football. Dog-friendly and family-friendly, with WiFi and offers.

Admiral Duncan London is a friendly pub with a “Local” atmosphere in the heart of the capital, on Old Compton Street. The venue is known for an eclectic mix of customers and a vibrant bar, and it hosts a range of event nights. The page highlights live entertainment such as Sunday Night Cabaret, Monday Night Karaoke, and weekly cabaret acts (with dates and times listed). It also notes features including Wi‑Fi and an outside area, and states it is an over-18s venue where ID may be requested on entry or at the bar.

Comptons London is a celebrated LGBTQIA+ venue on Old Compton Street, built on the site of the 200-year-old Swiss Hotel. It has been at the centre of the gay scene since 1986 and is described as a welcoming “Grande Dame” and a steadfast heart of gay Soho. The page highlights seasonal cocktails (“Front Row Pours”) and a busy programme of events, including DJ nights and themed socials. The venue also notes it is cask marque approved and offers real ale, with Wi‑Fi and a smoking area.

De Hems Dutch Cafe Bar is an authentic Dutch pub tucked away down a Soho side street, on the corner of Chinatown. It’s described as London’s one and only authentic Dutch pub, with deep history and tradition—formerly a watering hole for Dutch sailors and an unofficial HQ of the Dutch World War II resistance. The venue offers a laid-back, homely atmosphere with flavoursome food, an explorative drinks menu, and options for a lazy lunch or a family dinner. Table booking and table ordering are available online, and the page also links to food and events sections.

A restored Soho corner boozer with a proper pub feel downstairs and a grill room upstairs for proper comfort-food classics. Expect Guinness on tap, plus a menu built around hearty British dishes like steak and chips, seafood, and indulgent puddings such as sticky toffee. The place has old-school character—dark bar atmosphere, modern-art touches, and a private room for lock-ins and music gatherings (with phone filming banned). With food served upstairs and cooking focused in the grill room, it’s a great spot for a relaxed pint followed by a substantial meal.

column16: Duke Of Wellington London is a pub in Westminster at 77 Wardour Street, open from midday until late. The venue promotes “Front Row Pours” with limited-edition cocktail features and highlights its bar atmosphere. It also runs a busy events programme including DJ nights, bingo, and pub quiz. Facilities listed include real ale (Cask Marque Approved), HD screens, Wi‑Fi, accessible toilets, wheelchair access, and an outside area. The page also notes it is a dog-friendly pub and includes live entertainment.

The French House is an iconic Soho pub known for a warm welcome and a lively mix of actors, writers, artists and film-world regulars. It offers a choice of thirty champagnes and wines by the glass, and is described as a haven for conversation thanks to its “no music, no machines, no television and no mobile phones” rule. The bar is open Monday to Friday 11:30–11pm and Sundays 12pm–10:30pm, with drinks served on a first-come, first-served basis. An upstairs restaurant is available for lunch (midday–3pm) and dinner (6pm–9:30pm) with daily-changing menus and limited seating.

The Golden Lion Soho is a traditional yet modern Greene King pub just off Shaftesbury Avenue in London’s West End Theatre area. It’s a great spot to stop in after a show, with a welcoming atmosphere and a menu of pub classics and small plates, including Sunday roasts. The venue is set up for sports fans, with Sky Sports and TNT Sports, plus big-screen viewing for live football and rugby events like the Six Nations, and it also promotes live fixtures and match-day bookings. Facilities include WiFi and the Greene King Sport App, and it’s listed as dog and family friendly. There’s also mention of functions and a function room for celebrations.

A classic Irish pub in the heart of Soho on Wardour Street, known for its late-night live music and high-energy atmosphere. Expect a multi-level space that feels lively and social, with bands and DJs keeping the night moving from early evening drinks through to late-night crowds. A great stop when you want more than a quiet pint—this is built for staying, listening and soaking up the buzz near Leicester Square.

column16: The Royal George is a pub in Charing Cross, London, described as one of Soho’s hidden gems with “dazzling interiors” and “quirky décor”. It offers classic pub food, craft beers and an “authentic, homely atmosphere”. The venue is positioned for catch-ups and get-togethers, and it also hosts open mic nights. It’s set near major landmarks including Leicester Square, The National Gallery, The British Museum and the River Thames, making it a convenient stop for a laid-back drinking and dining experience.

Rupert Street Bar London is a chic LGBTQIA+ bar in Soho, with a gorgeous interior for celebrations and cocktails. The venue is known for legendary weekend vibes, hosted by queer DJs and performers, and it offers a cocktail menu including limited-edition seasonal drinks. The page also lists upcoming drag cabaret and DJ events. Facilities mentioned include HD screens, a cocktail menu, live music, an outside area, smoking area, beer garden, and dog-friendly policy, alongside accessibility features like wheelchair access and accessible toilets.

column16: The Coach & Horses is one of Soho’s oldest pubs, dating back to 1731. Set in the heart of London’s Theatreland on the corner of Old Compton Street and Charing Cross Road, it’s a cosy, characterful spot for pre-theatre drinks or a break while exploring. The pub offers a wide selection of cask ales and lagers, plus a carefully selected wine list and traditional spirits. It also highlights its historic Grade II listed building and notes that Shepherd Neame restored the original name as part of a major refurbishment. The venue is open every day and available to hire for events throughout the year.

The Coach & Horses, Soho is a historic London pub with a well-stocked bar offering modern craft beers and cask classics. It’s described as a deeply loved London institution with rich history, and it’s voted Evening Standard’s number 1 pub to visit in London. The venue welcomes families and assistance dogs, offers free WiFi, and has outside seating. It also states “Dog Friendly” and provides step-free access. The page notes limited capacity and that the pub does not take table bookings, welcoming walk-ins instead.

The Crown & Two Chairmen in London combines British pub hospitality with “individuality, character and quirky charm”. It’s positioned as a laid-back yet memorable place for drinking and dining, with an explorative drinks menu and “tempting and flavoursome food”. The page also highlights ways to book a table online, order from your seat, and buy gift cards. Opening hours are listed for every day, and the venue is located at 31–32 Dean Street, London (W1D 3SB).

The Dog and Duck is a historic, Grade II listed pub in Soho with a rich story dating back to 1734, and a present building built in 1897 by architect Francis Cannon. The pub is known for its exquisite period interior, including thousands of glazed tiles, mahogany panelling, and decorative mirrors. It’s also associated with famous visitors such as George Orwell, John Constable, Dante Gabriel Rossetti, and Madonna. The pub offers British pub classics with “perfect pints and unbeatable pies”, with food available via its menus and the option to order at table or book a table. Opening hours run from midday through the evening.

Welcome to Flying Horse, a historic pub in Tottenham Court Road (Oxford Street, London). The page describes it as a traditional pub with unique character, known for an eclectic range of real ales served with a generous measure of British hospitality. It also promotes British pub classic menus with “unbeatable pies” and tempting dishes, and offers options to book a table, order at table, and buy gift cards. The venue is positioned as being within a short stroll of Tottenham Court Road, Charing Cross Road and New Oxford Street.

The Lyric is Soho’s local, described as the area’s oldest independent free house near Piccadilly Circus. It offers craft beer, real cask ales, fine wines, and pub classics including fish and chips and Sunday roasts, with a warm, friendly welcome. The pub is set in a cosy ambience and invites visitors to relax while catching live sports.

The Montagu Pyke is a Wetherspoon pub on Charing Cross Road (also at 20 Greek Street) in Westminster. The building’s main frontage was originally Pyke’s Cambridge Circus Cinematograph Theatre, built in 1911; after a fire in 1915 it was restored as the Super cinema, later becoming the Tatler, Filmcenta and the three-screen Cannon. In 1988 it became the Marquee Club, closing in 1996. Today it offers TV screens and step-free access, with music mentioned in the facilities list. The pub serves children’s meals and has a children’s menu, and it’s open from early morning through late evening.

The Queen’s Head is an independent free house near Piccadilly Circus in Soho, serving real ales since 1736. It’s a characterful pub with an upstairs room available for exclusive hire for up to 50 guests, ideal for pre-theatre drinks and after-work pints. Walk-ins are welcome, with reservations recommended for groups of 6+. The pub is described as a drinks-only venue with no kitchen and no food service. Live music runs every Sunday from 7pm with no booking needed and no cover charge. It’s located just outside Exit 1 of Piccadilly Circus tube station on Denman Street.

The Spice of Life is a pub in the heart of Soho, described as a classic pub with old-school charm and Soho’s lively spirit. It offers hearty pub classics, small plates for sharing, and a bar serving craft beers, fine wines and cocktails. The venue also has a Backstage Cellar Bar and hosts live gigs and vibrant events. Alongside the pub, it offers boutique rooms, with guests encouraged to linger in the mornings and enjoy nights out in Soho.

The Three Greyhounds is a historic pub in Soho, London, described as a place for “perfect pints” and “unbeatable pies”. It offers British pub classic menus with tempting dishes, and guests can book a table or order at table. The page also highlights loyalty and ale & gin trails, and notes the pub’s convenient location near Tottenham Court Road and Leicester Square Underground Stations, Soho Square Gardens and Chinatown, with many major attractions nearby.

Waxy O’Connor’s is an award-winning Irish bar on Rupert Street at the edge of Soho. It’s described as a labyrinth of four unique bars over six levels, each with its own atmosphere, centred around the famous Waxy’s tree. The pub offers a home-made bar menu of food served all day, with meals and snacks available. There’s plenty going on, including live music sessions and live sport with dedicated fanzone areas for sports such as Irish GAA, rugby, football, horseracing, tennis and golf. The venue also hosts events like St Patrick’s Day and weekly live music.

Waxy’s Little Sister is an award-winning Irish bar in London offering a warm Irish welcome and a more chilled alternative to Waxy O’Connor’s. The venue has comfy sofas, open fires and a relaxing vibe, spread over two floors with a Dumb Waiter upstairs. It’s a place to meet friends, grab a quick drink or settle in for the evening. The site also highlights events and “What’s On”, including live sport coverage such as the Six Nations and Live GAA with multiple screens, plus seasonal events like St Patrick’s Day. There are also options for private parties/private hire.

column16: Glasshouse Stores offers pub classics and some lighter dishes, with menus available online. The drinks section highlights Samuel Smith’s beers brewed at the Old Brewery in Tadcaster (founded in 1758), including cask Old Brewery Bitter served from oak casks in the pub cellar, plus house wines and a selection of spirits. The venue also supports private hire for parties and social gatherings, with party bite offers and buffet menus. A “Darts Package” is advertised, including darts, food and drinks, and sharing boards.

The Green Man is a historic pub in the heart of Soho, London. The page highlights a heritage of 150+ years and focuses on “perfect pints” and “unbeatable pies”, with British pub classic menus and tempting dishes. You can book a table, order at table, or walk in. It’s described as being well placed for central London attractions, and is a short walk from Oxford Circus and Tottenham Court Road tube stations, with many other nearby stations listed. The page also promotes loyalty rewards and ale & gin trails.

Kings Arms Oxford Street is described as Soho’s oldest gay bar, with a long and proud history as a safe space for the LGBTQIA+ community. It’s a favourite with the Bear community and is affectionately known as “The KA”. The venue offers a well-stocked bar and traditional charm, plus regular entertainment including guest and resident DJs at weekends and “Legendary Bearaoke” (running for over 25 years). The page also highlights cask marque-approved real ale, HD screens, Wi‑Fi, a function area, and a late licence, alongside a dog-friendly policy and a smoking area.

Mr Fogg’s Hat Tavern is a lively Victorian tavern in Soho, London, set across two floors on Great Chapel Street. It offers a social drinking experience with a lower-ground Saloon Bar and a well-stocked bar serving draught beers and ales, classic cocktails, and signature punches. The venue is known for its curious collection of millinery and quirky details, creating a characterful setting that feels distinct from the ordinary Soho pub. It’s positioned for pre- or post-theatre drinks and group occasions, with space for up to 110 guests. The page also mentions live sports screenings “occasionally”.

O’Neill’s on Carnaby Street is an original Irish pub in London with a warm Irish welcome and a lively atmosphere. The venue offers a big night out, plus options for lunch and breakfast. The page highlights “great food” alongside live sport, and mentions fantastic music, drinks offers, and live experiences across sport, music and events. It also promotes table booking and ordering for collection, suggesting food service alongside drinks. Located at 37–38 Great Marlborough Street, it’s positioned as being in the heart of the action in London, with opening hours running from late morning into the evening.

column16: The Sun & 13 Cantons is a historic, eclectic and vibrant pub in Soho, with a great drinks range including craft beers from independent breweries. It also offers food via Mamapen, its resident Cambodian kitchen, described as London’s only Cambodian restaurant, with bookings available Tuesday–Saturday (12pm–9pm). The venue includes a basement bar for private events such as business meetings and celebrations, plus a well-stocked bar and outside seating. Facilities include free WiFi, air conditioning, and assistance dogs welcome. It’s located at 21 Great Pulteney Street, London W1F 9NG, with waterside setting mentioned.

The Argyll Arms is a historic, Grade II listed Victorian pub in Oxford Circus, dating back to 1868. It’s known for an ornate interior with original features such as mirrored walls and decorative ceilings, plus decorative etched glass partitions. The pub’s bar was originally divided to separate social classes, but today everyone is welcome. Named after the second Duke of Argyll, the story includes rumours of a secret tunnel that once connected the pub to the Duke’s nearby mansion. The pub offers British pub classic menus with “unbeatable pies” and “tempting dishes”, and provides table booking and ordering options.

The Blue Posts is a small, authentic British pub in the heart of Soho (22 Berwick St, London). The page highlights events and encourages visitors not to miss what’s going on, with a link to the full events list. It’s described as a great spot for after-dinner drinks, with “proper bit of old Soho” vibes and positive comments about the staff. Opening hours are shown for each day of the week (generally 11:30–23:00, with Sunday closing at 22:30).

Welcome to Crown, Brewer Street, a historic pub in Soho. The page describes it as a traditional pub with unique character, known for an eclectic range of real ales and quality pub food. It also highlights “perfect pints” and “unbeatable pies,” served with generous British hospitality. Visitors can book a table, order at table, and there are promotions such as loyalty and ale & gin trails. The location is described as being on Brewer Street in London, within a short stroll of Regent Street, Shaftesbury Avenue and Piccadilly Circus.

The Ganton Arms is a bustling bar & kitchen in Soho, just off Carnaby Street in London’s West End. It serves classic lagers and craft beers, plus a premium range of wines and spirits. Food is a key part of the venue, with a seasonal menu created by an executive chef and kitchen team, including small plates and crowd-pleasers such as salt & pepper squid and a Philly steak wrap. The pub also highlights its fish & chips and a Sunday roast featuring a 28-day aged sirloin. There’s also a hidden upstairs secret cocktail bar with velvet booths and curated playlists.

Originally built in 1727 and extended in 1897, The George wears its history with pride. Stunning original features make this one of Soho’s must-visit sports, music, and food pubs – and most of the locals agree!

column16: A classic Soho boozer on Broadwick Street, known for Sam Smith’s ales and a strong value menu. Inside, the downstairs bar is split into three separate drinking areas, while upstairs offers more space and a different feel. Named after local doctor John Snow, with a nod to his cholera research in the area. With long opening hours most days, it’s a straightforward spot for a pint and a relaxed wander through Soho’s pub life.

column16: Tucked just off Carnaby Street, this historic back-street pub has a cosy, vintage feel with dark panelling, a long wooden bar and a warm coal-effect fire. By night it’s lively with locals, groups and football fans, with music and sports TV kept at conversation-friendly volume. Food is served throughout the week with classic pub choices like sandwiches, chips and burgers, plus jacket potatoes and a home-made chilli. With an upstairs room for busier evenings and private functions, it’s a welcoming Soho stop that still feels properly pubby.

column16: The Shakespeare’s Head is a historic pub in London’s Soho, rumoured to have once been owned by the Shakespeare family, with a bust of the playwright at the front. It offers a pub food menu with seasonal specials and a Sunday roast, alongside a wide drinks range and Greene King beers. The venue has a beer garden (weather permitting) and is set up for functions, private dining, and group visits. It’s also a sports-focused pub, showing live rugby (Six Nations) and live football with Sky Sports and TNT Sports, plus big-screen match-day atmosphere. Dogs are welcome, and the pub is family friendly.

The Shaston Arms is an intimate free house pub and kitchen in the heart of Soho, just a short walk from Oxford Circus and Carnaby Street. It offers London beers, real ale and a concise wine list, alongside a seasonally focused kitchen with grilled meat, seafood, a daily specials board, snacks and sharing plates. The pub has traditional booths, bookable dining tables and a large outside space that catches the afternoon sun, creating a hidden-gem feel in Central London. It’s also described as a sister pub to Waterman’s Arms in Barnes.

The Ship is a lively Soho pub at the heart of the Soho music scene. It’s described as relaxed at lunchtime, then “starts rocking” when the sun goes down, with an eclectic mix of music and a vibrant atmosphere. The pub offers dining with a selection of delicious toasties, and it has a well-stocked bar featuring modern craft beers and cask classics. It’s also listed as a historic pub, and assistance dogs are welcome. The venue is located at 116 Wardour Street, Soho, London (W1F 0TT).

The White Horse is a historic pub in Soho, located on Newburgh Street near Carnaby Street. Dating back to the early 1700s, it was rebuilt in the 1930s with a striking art deco exterior, plus two original stained glass pub signs in the balcony ironwork showing a prancing white horse. The pub is described as a great city-centre spot to catch up with friends, relax with family, and enjoy “perfect pints and unbeatable pies” alongside dishes on British pub classic menus. It also highlights its central location among shops and nearby attractions.

Inn 1888 is a beautiful Victorian pub in Devonshire Street, just off Marylebone High Street. Built in 1898 (originally called The Devonshire Arms), it has been refurbished while preserving original features such as majolica wall tiles, etched mirrors and half stained-glass windows. The pub has two open fires, and a large basement that was used as a firing range by the Ministry of Defence during both world wars. As a free house, it offers draughts, a guest cask ale, spirits (including London Gins) and a wine list. It also serves freshly made pizza, with a dedicated pizza menu.

On at least one Friday visit, food wasn’t being served that evening, though bar snacks like pork scratchings and scampi fries were available.

column16: The Lord Wargrave is a smokehouse and whisky bar in Marylebone, with a cosy restaurant area and a bar boasting over 200 whiskies. It serves an authentic barbecue menu and Sunday roasts, with meats smoked in-house low and slow over British hickory logs. The menu includes options for vegans and vegetarians, such as a plant-based burger and other sides. The Bloomsbury Tavern is an historic Grade II listed pub in Holborn, dating back to 1856. It’s known for its dark hangman’s history, once described as the final watering hole en route to the noose at Marble Arch, but today it offers a more welcoming atmosphere. The pub is well placed for visiting the British Museum, Covent Garden and Theatreland, making it a convenient pitstop for lunch, a post-work pint or a weekend visit. Inside, stained glass windows add natural light and ambience. The venue serves Shepherd Neame ales on tap, an extensive wine selection, and fresh food served all day. It also highlights live sport on TV.

Facilities include being dog friendly, family friendly, and offering WiFi and a historic pub setting. There are also references to big match viewing with big screens for events like the World Cup, plus general “what’s on” activities. Reviews mention a Sunday roast and a good atmosphere.

A small Sam Smiths pub tucked just off New Oxford Street, handy for the theatres and the British Museum. Step inside to find a proper local feel, with friendly staff, regulars at the bar and traditional wooden partitions that create cosy “separate rooms”. There’s also a small outdoor beer garden by the road for a pint on warmer days. Expect pre-theatre dinner and drinks, plus a straightforward, well-kept West End pub atmosphere.

column16: The Garrick Arms in Charing Cross is a family-friendly pub restaurant with a pre-theatre bite to eat. The menu includes pub classics such as mac & cheese, hearty pies and a stacked burger, plus small plates and Sunday roasts with classic trimmings. The venue also promotes booking for tables and highlights “Cheers to Good Drinks” with a range of drinks. Facilities mentioned include being dog friendly and having WiFi. The page also references big screens for the World Cup and “What’s On” events, suggesting a lively atmosphere for getting together.

The Imperial Soho is a traditional, historic and cosy pub in the heart of Soho, right next to Leicester Square and Chinatown. It’s a family-friendly place to enjoy cask ales and wines, with a welcoming atmosphere for a day out or an evening in. The pub has a beer garden (weather permitting) and offers a menu worth discovering, including pub classics and a Sunday roast with all the classic trimmings. It’s also a sports-focused venue, with Sky Sports and TNT Sports, and it shows major rugby and live football events. Facilities include WiFi and dog-friendly access.

The Long Acre Covent Garden is a fresh, modern bar with the charm of a local pub, ideally located between Covent Garden, Trafalgar Square and Leicester Square. It offers a varied menu for quick bites or a longer night out with friends. The venue also has a downstairs area called The LA Club for dancing late into the night. Facilities include Wi‑Fi, accessible toilets, a smoking area, children welcome, and a function area. It’s set up for sports viewing with HD screens and multiple sports brands, and it lists live music and live entertainment. There’s also an outside area and it’s dog friendly.

The Moon Under Water in Milton Keynes is part of the Xscape leisure complex. Built on a greenfield site, it was officially opened to the public in 2000, and features a distinctive 44-metre-high structure that stands out on the Milton Keynes skyline. The pub offers Wi‑Fi, TV screens, and a licensed outside area (deck), with step-free access and a baby changing station. It serves food, including children’s meals, and encourages ordering food and drinks to your table via the Wetherspoon app. Opening times run from early mornings through late nights, with later closing on Fridays and Saturdays.

The Porcupine is a historic pub in Leicester Square, London, described as a traditional venue with a unique character. It’s known for an eclectic range of real ales and quality pub food, served with “famous British hospitality”. The page also highlights the pub’s focus on perfect pints and “unbeatable pies”, with tempting dishes on British pub classic menus. Visitors can book a table or order at table, and there are loyalty and ale & gin trail promotions mentioned on the page.

A Covent Garden lounge-bar with a retro feel and plenty of natural light from large windows. Expect award-winning pies from Pieminister, plus classic pub snacks like sausage rolls and pork scratchings. Food is served Monday to Saturday from midday to 10pm, with dine-in and takeout options. For game nights, you can catch the big game on BT Sport, join Poker Night, or play darts. There’s also space for birthdays and special events, including the option to hire the whole room.

It’s close to the Palace Theatre and Covent Garden Underground Station, and offers a warm, welcoming pub atmosphere with a bar and restaurant seating. The venue highlights “Delicious Pub Food,” including small plates, pub classics, and a traditional Sunday Roast with classic trimmings. There’s also a “What’s On” section for events, plus promotions like World Cup bookings and “big screens at the ready.” Facilities listed include WiFi, disabled facilities, and it’s dog and family friendly.

Tucked beneath the arches of Charing Cross, this cosy cellar bar feels like an old-world hideaway with exposed brick, wood panelling, intimate alcoves and candlelit tables. Expect an extensive cellar and a strong drinks focus, including craft beers, spirits and Davy’s Old Wallop served in pewter tankards or copper jugs. Classic British food is available from bar and dining room menus using seasonal ingredients. A great choice for relaxed evenings, with space for parties, meetings and private dinners.

column16: Set inside the Corinthia on Northumberland Avenue, this Tom Kerridge-led bar and grill pairs a sleek, high-ceilinged dining room with a proper bar and lounge. Expect a serious food focus—starters, mains and desserts plus a bar menu—alongside a cocktail-led drinks list. There’s also an al fresco first-floor terrace pop-up (Velvet Alfresco) and a standout, space-and-intimacy feel with tables spaced for conversation. Ideal for a polished night out when you want great cooking, attentive service and a stylish central-London setting.

column16: Mr Fogg’s Tavern at 58 St. Martin’s Lane is a theatrical “upstairs downstairs” venue with a Victorian tavern on the ground floor and a refined gin parlour and salon upstairs. The downstairs space has a warm wooden interior with nineteenth-century artifacts and a large aviary filled with plants, stuffed birds and oddities. Staff serve real ales, batch brews, gin cocktails and grog, and there’s “honest fare” served throughout the day and evening, including “The Finest Pie in London Town” and roast game, fowl and beast. Upstairs features antique theatrical props, wigs and old scripts, plus a large selection of gins and tonics.

Set in Hungerford House on the Victoria Embankment, this riverside bar is a popular late-night stop with a view over the Thames. Expect cocktails, beer and wine, plus pub-style food such as sharer platters and bar snacks. The venue is split into distinct spaces including the Blanca Bar and Club Noir, with party tunes and live music listed—ideal for after-work drinks, birthdays and group nights out. With late opening hours through the week, it’s built for staying out in the heart of London.

column16: The Princess Of Wales is a historic pub in Charing Cross, named in memory of George IV’s secret first wife. The page highlights the pub’s heritage and positions it as a place for “perfect pints” and “unbeatable pies”, with tempting dishes on British pub classic menus. It also mentions ways to dine in or order, including booking a table, ordering at the table, and collection. The venue is located on Villiers Street, with background on the street name.

The Harp is a blissfully traditional British ale house in London’s Covent Garden, described as a historic pub known for great beer and good conversation. It’s also well known for traditional ciders and perries from around the country. The well-stocked bar offers modern craft beers alongside cask classics. The pub has a private room for event bookings, with external catering allowed (it notes it does not have a kitchen). The venue welcomes walk-ins (no table bookings) and offers free WiFi. Assistance dogs are welcome and it’s listed as dog friendly.

The Lemon Tree in Covent Garden is a welcoming pub tucked away in the heart of Covent Garden, offering a respite from West London’s bustle. It’s known for authentic Thai cuisine with homemade dishes prepared fresh to order, with options including vegetables or tofu, plus a limited selection of traditional pub fare. The venue also serves an extensive range of premium spirits (gins, rums, vodkas and whiskies), fine wines, and outstanding real ales. There’s a function room available for corporate meetings or private parties, making it suitable for both afternoons and nights out.

The Marquis is Covent Garden’s “Rock n Roll Watering Hole”, a lively London pub with a vinyl-lover vibe and a vast record collection. It’s described as a hub for live music, supporting local talent with musicians, bands and DJs five nights a week, and it has hosted notable moments such as a surprise Green Day gig in 2023. For food, the upstairs bar and dining area “Fagin’s Den” offers home-cooked meals, with a British pub menu and buffet options for groups. The pub is open daily with later hours on Friday and Saturday, and also offers exclusive hire of the upstairs bar for at least 20 guests.

Retro Bar London is a hidden gem tucked away down an alley in the West End, described as one of the area’s friendliest gay venues. It occupies a site that has been a pub since the 17th century and has been a secret haven for the LGBTQIA+ community since the 90s. The bar is known for Insta-friendly rock ’n’ roll “gallery” walls and an eclectic jukebox covering everything from disco to sleazy beats. The page also highlights limited-edition cocktails and lists upcoming events such as Busy Lady Bingo. There’s a phone booking option and the venue notes features like Wi‑Fi, a function area, an outside area, and a dog-friendly policy.

The Round House in Covent Garden has a distinctive rounded facade and a cosy interior. It’s known for a lively atmosphere and a wide selection of drinks, from modern craft beers to cask classics. The pub is described as historic and offers a covered smoking area and outside seating. Facilities include step-free access, baby changing facilities, free WiFi, and assistance dogs welcome. Food is served daily with set food times, making it a good spot for a classic British pub visit in the heart of Covent Garden.

The Salisbury is a historic pub in Covent Garden, built in 1899 and described as a famous celeb hangout since the 1960s. It’s a Grade II listed 18th-century pub with traditional etched glass, gold chandeliers and hand-carved mahogany panels, plus ornate woodwork and chesterfield-style leather seating. There’s an open-plan beer garden out front, and the pub is positioned near major attractions like Leicester Square, Piccadilly Circus and Trafalgar Square. Food is served alongside cask ales and classic pub dishes, including battered fish, sausages, pie and mash, with roast Sunday roast on Sundays. The pub is family-friendly and dog-friendly, with free WiFi.

The Sherlock Holmes, St James's is one of London’s original themed pubs, offering a “pocket of Victoriana” in modern London. With a history dating back centuries, it’s a warm, characterful inn near major landmarks and The Playhouse Theatre. The pub serves traditional pub food with a menu covering snacks, sharers, starters, sandwiches, mains and puddings, plus lunch options and Sunday roasts. There’s a well-stocked bar with cask ales, craft beers, fine wines, cocktails and hot drinks. Facilities include WiFi, disabled access, and it’s dog and family friendly. Guests can also sit outside on the roof terrace.

The Ship & Shovell is a traditional pub near Charing Cross, set just moments from central London landmarks. It has historic charm and a lively atmosphere, split across two unique buildings either side of Craven Passage, with the buildings connected underground by a shared cellar. The pub dates back to the 17th century and is believed to be the only UK pub split across two buildings connected this way. Today it’s run by Lou and her team, offering a drinks selection including signature Badger and Outland beers, plus a pub food menu featuring dishes such as hearty pies, classic Fish & Chips, and burgers.

Set on the Strand near Charing Cross, this modern, West End-sized pub feels surprisingly calm at quieter times. It’s built around a strong beer focus, with Czech Budvar in several styles plus rotating guest beers on keg and cask. Expect a technical, tap-focused approach to serving, with hand-washed glasses and a foamy pour. Food changes regularly as different groups take over the kitchen—at the time of writing it’s Gyoza Paradox—so there’s always something new to try.

column16: The Nell Gwynne is a historic London pub in the heart of Covent Garden, described as a timeless landmark “Est. 1667” built on the site of the Old Bull Inn. Named after Nell Gwynne, it’s set just off the Strand and is presented as a charming, cosy hidden treasure with a lively atmosphere. The pub serves British bar snacks such as hearty pies and premium sausage rolls, plus a summer spritz selection. It also highlights a Free Jukebox for choosing the soundtrack. There’s a “Watch the FIFA World Cup 2026 with us” section promoting a sporting matchday atmosphere.

Savoy Tap is a traditional pub in the City of Westminster, tucked away down a quiet street off the Strand near Aldwych and The Strand. It offers a warm welcome and a “perfect pint”, with an extensive range of cask ales, lagers, and premium wines and spirits. The pub has been recently refurbished with a stylish new interior while retaining original features such as beautiful stained-glass leaded windows. It’s also available to book for functions, from birthday parties to work gatherings. The venue has a varied history over the last 300 years, with names including Savoy Barracks and New Savoy Tavern, and it became Savoy Tap in 2018.

column16: The Cheshire Cheese is a Grade II listed pub of great character in London, described as a hidden treasure near the Royal Courts of Justice and the Inns of Court. There has been a pub here since at least the late 18th century, while the current building dates from 1926 and is in the interwar school of design, designed by pub architect Nowell Parr Senior. The pub offers a wide range of cask ales and lagers, an extensive wine list, and a delicious menu. It also highlights a function room and WiFi, with the River Thames just minutes away.

The Coal Hole is an historic, Grade II listed pub on the Strand, built in 1903 by architect T.E Collcutt as part of the Savoy Court extension of the Savoy Hotel complex. The site is rumoured to have been the coal cellar for the Savoy Hotel. In Victorian times it was a popular “song and supper” club, and in the Edwardian era Gilbert and Sullivan frequently performed there. The pub is also linked to the Wolf Club started by Edmund Keane. Today it’s a unique city-centre pub close to London’s theatres, with a focus on perfect pints and British pub classic menus including “unbeatable pies”.

Facilities include WiFi, and it’s described as dog-friendly and family-friendly. The pub also offers functions and venue hire, including packages for business events, parties and weddings, plus a private dining room upstairs.

Porterhouse in Covent Garden is a large, family-owned pub split over three main floors with three bars and mezzanine levels. It serves craft beer and “quality pub grub”, with a menu including fish & chips, burgers, pizzas and homemade Sunday roasts, plus vegetarian, vegan and gluten-free options. The venue also has one of Central London’s largest beer gardens and a Terrace. Sports fans can watch major sporting events (especially rugby) on 18 screens. Live music is held in the Basement Bar every Thursday, Friday and Saturday with house bands playing rock and pop covers.

The Wellington is an historic pub on The Strand, dating back to 1903. It’s known for its stunning neo-gothic interiors, including a sculpted ground-floor ceiling, stained glass windows, and a large, cosy original marble fireplace. The pub is presented as a place for “perfect pints” and British pub classic menus, with tempting dishes and options to book a table or order at the table/for collection.
